      "body": "Office365CalendarService.createEvent uses `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and builds the URL from `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId`. When EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents calls createEvent once per destination calendar entry (each with a different credentialId), the Office365 service ignores the credentialId parameter (the interface now requires it but this implementation's signature is still `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)` — it doesn't even declare the second parameter). So for host B's credential, the service still uses the FIRST destination calendar's externalId (host A's calendar) with host B's access token — either failing auth or creating the event on the wrong calendar. The service must use the credentialId to find the matching destination calendar entry, like GoogleCalendarService does."
    },
    {
      "file": "packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts",
      "line": 94,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "bug",

      "body": "Office365CalendarService.updateEvent (line 94-109) always uses `/me/calendar/events/${uid}` and deleteEvent (line 111-123) always uses `/me/calendar/events/${uid}`, ignoring both the `externalCalendarId` parameter and `event.destinationCalendar`. For users who have their events on a non-default calendar (which is exactly what destinationCalendar is for), updates and deletes will 404 or hit the wrong calendar. This was pre-existing behavior but becomes more impactful with the multi-destination-calendar change: for collective events, the event may live on a host's non-default Office365 calendar, and update/delete will silently fail to find it. The methods should use externalCalendarId when provided: `/me/calendars/${externalCalendarId}/events/${uid}`."

    {

However, in many call sites the destination calendar objects come from partial selects (e.g. `user.destinationCalendar` selected without `credential` include, or `booking.destinationCalendar` selected as a scalar relation). The Prisma `DestinationCalendar` type includes all scalar fields, which is fine, but code that does `destination.credentialId` (EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents line 340) relies on credentialId being present — it is a scalar on the model so it's fine. The concern is that `IntegrationCalendar` (used in CalendarManager.getConnectedCalendars) is a different shape, and some code mixes them. The type is technically correct for the Prisma relation but the class is also used with IntegrationCalendar-like objects in places; consider using a narrower type like `Pick<DestinationCalendar, \"id\" | \"externalId\" | \"integration\" | \"credentialId\">[]` to make the contract explicit. The Booking model has a single `destinationCalendarId` foreign key, so only the first (organizer's) destination calendar is stored. The additional team hosts' destination calendars pushed into evt.destinationCalendar (teamDestinationCalendars) are used during event creation (EventManager.create) but are NOT persisted on the booking. On reschedule or cancel, handlers reconstruct evt.destinationCalendar from `booking.destinationCalendar` (single) — the other hosts' calendars are lost. This means the multi-host calendar support works only for the initial creation; reschedule/cancel will not update/delete events on the other hosts' calendars (unless references are used, but handleCancelBooking's evt construction doesn't aggregate from references). ```

findings.title: updateEvent/deleteEvent look up destination calendar by externalId instead of credentialId, always yielding undefined
findings.body: In updateEvent (line 254-256) and deleteEvent (line 315-317), the fallback when externalCalendarId is not provided is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. Since externalCalendarId is falsy in that branch, `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId` compares a string to undefined/null and can never match, so selectedCalendar/calendarId is always undefined and the code silently falls back to "primary" (update) or "primary" (delete). For collective events where the event lives on a host's non-primary calendar, reschedule/cancel will target the wrong calendar (or fail with 404 which is swallowed in deleteEvent), leaving stale events on the real calendar. The lookup should match by credentialId (as createEvent does at line 147-149) or the caller should always pass externalCalendarId.

findings.title: Hangout-link patch uses possibly-undefined selectedCalendar as calendarId
findings.body: In createEvent, after `calendar.events.insert` succeeds, the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` (line 166-177) uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` directly. selectedCalendar is `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.credentialId === credentialId)?.externalId`, which is undefined when no destination calendar matches the credential (the insert then correctly used `selectedCalendar || "primary"` at line 154). Passing `calendarId: undefined` to the patch call will make the Google API request fail or hit an invalid endpoint, so the Meet hangout link is never written into the event description for hosts whose destination calendar entry doesn't carry a matching credentialId. It should use `selectedCalendar || "primary"` like the insert does.

findings.title: Google Meet fallback check crashes or misfires because mainHostDestinationCalendar may be undefined
findings.body: In EventManager.create, line 118-120: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` then `if (evt.location === MeetLocationType && mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar")`. When `evt.destinationCalendar` is null/undefined or an empty array, mainHostDestinationCalendar is undefined and accessing `.integration` throws a TypeError, aborting event creation entirely for any Google Meet booking without a destination calendar. Even when defined, checking only the first destination calendar means a collective event whose first host uses Office365 but a later host uses Google Calendar will be incorrectly downgraded to Cal Video. The check should be `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"` (optional chaining) and ideally check whether ANY destination calendar is google_calendar.

findings.title: createAllCalendarEvents only creates events for destination calendars, dropping other hosts' calendars and other_calendar integrations for collective events
findings.body: The rewritten createAllCalendarEvents iterates `event.destinationCalendar` and creates one event per destination entry. However, for collective team events the PR's own handleNewBooking change pushes each host's destinationCalendar into evt.destinationCalendar, but the EventManager is constructed with only the organizer's credentials (`new EventManager(user)` in handleNewBooking). Inside the loop, when `destination.credentialId` is set, the code looks up the credential in `this.calendarCredentials` and, if not found, fetches it from the DB — that part is OK. But when `destination.credentialId` is NOT set (DestinationCalendar rows always have credentialId in the Prisma schema, but the type allows it to be absent), the else branch filters `this.calendarCredentials` by `destination.integration` — the organizer's credentials only — so a non-organizer host's calendar type won't be found and no event is created for that host. Additionally, the trailing block that creates events for all `other_calendar` credentials runs regardless, which is fine, but the primary per-host creation depends on the organizer's credential list containing every host's calendar credential, which it does not. The net effect: for collective events, hosts other than the organizer may never get calendar events created, which is exactly what issue #7754 is about.

findings.title: Fallback when no destinationCalendar filters by type === "calendar" which matches no real credential type
findings.body: In createAllCalendarEvents, the else branch (no destinationCalendar) does `this.calendarCredentials.filter((cred) => cred.type === "calendar")`. Real credential types are values like "google_calendar", "office365_calendar", "caldav_calendar" — none equals the literal "calendar". So when a user has no destination calendar configured, no calendar event is created at all (previously the code had the same filter, but combined with the destinationCalendar branch this means users without a destination calendar silently get no calendar event). The fallback should pick the first calendar credential (e.g. `[0]`) or filter by `cred.type.endsWith("_calendar")`.

findings.title: updateAllCalendarEvents pushes promises into result array inside a for-loop without awaiting, mixing awaited and pending promises
findings.body: In updateAllCalendarEvents, the loop `for (const reference of calendarReference) { ... result.push(updateEvent(credential, event, bookingRefUid, calenderExternalId)); ... }` pushes unawaited promises, and `return Promise.all(result)` at line 590 awaits them — that part is fine. However, when `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found in `this.calendarCredentials` and the DB fetch also fails (credentialFromDB null or app slug missing), `credential` remains undefined and `updateEvent(undefined, ...)` is called, which will throw inside updateEvent when it does `getCalendar(credential)` / accesses credential properties. The catch block at line 591 then converts this into a generic failure for ALL references, marking every calendar update as failed even though other references may have succeeded. A missing/deleted credential for one host should fail only that reference, not abort the whole batch.

findings.title: Booking.destinationCalendar connect only persists the first destination calendar, dropping additional hosts' calendars for collective events
findings.body: When creating the booking record, the code does `destinationCalendar: evt.destinationCalendar && evt.destinationCalendar.length > 0 ? { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } } : undefined`. The Booking model has a single destinationCalendar relation, so only the organizer's (first) destination calendar is persisted on the booking. The additional team hosts' destination calendars that were pushed into `evt.destinationCalendar` (teamDestinationCalendars) exist only on the in-memory CalendarEvent. On reschedule/cancel, handlers like handleCancelBooking build `destinationCalendar` from `bookingToDelete.destinationCalendar` (single) or `user.destinationCalendar`, so the extra hosts' calendars are lost and their calendar events won't be updated/deleted correctly. This is a data-integrity gap: the multi-host support only works at creation time, not on reschedule/cancel, unless references (which do store per-credential externalCalendarId/credentialId) are used — but handleCancelBooking's evt construction ignores references for destinationCalendar.

findings.title: teamDestinationCalendars only collected for COLLECTIVE scheduling, silently dropping host calendars for ROUND_ROBIN
findings.body: The code `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE" && user.destinationCalendar) { teamDestinationCalendars.push(user.destinationCalendar); }` and later `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE") { evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars); }` restricts multi-host destination calendars to COLLECTIVE events only. For ROUND_ROBIN team events (where a single host is chosen per booking), the chosen host may not be the organizer (users[0]), so the event is created on the organizer's calendar instead of the assigned host's calendar. The PR description says "supports multiple so host can get invited correctly" — round-robin hosts are equally affected. Either include ROUND_ROBIN here or ensure the round-robin-selected host's destination calendar is used.

findings.title: Cancellation loops over all calendar references but deletes using each reference's uid against every user calendar credential, causing wrong/extra deletions for collective events
findings.body: The new cancellation logic iterates `bookingCalendarReference` (all references with type containing "_calendar"). For each reference with a credentialId, it resolves the calendar and calls `calendar?.deleteEvent(uid, evt, externalCalendarId)` — that's correct per-reference. But in the recurring branch (lines 449-461) and in the no-credentialId branch (lines 473-482), it iterates ALL of `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` filtered by `_calendar` and deletes `bookingRef.uid` from each — for a collective booking with 2 hosts, the organizer's credential list only contains the organizer's calendars, so the second host's calendar event is never deleted (stale event remains). Conversely, for a single user with multiple calendar credentials connected, the same uid is deleted from every connected calendar, which may delete events that were never created (harmless due to 404 handling, but noisy). The deletion should be driven by the booking references (which store credentialId + externalCalendarId per calendar event), not by the organizer's full credential list.

findings.title: Cancel evt.destinationCalendar only includes booking/user destination calendar, not all hosts' calendars, so calendar services pick the wrong calendar for collective events
findings.body: The evt built for cancellation sets `destinationCalendar: bookingToDelete?.destinationCalendar ? [bookingToDelete?.destinationCalendar] : bookingToDelete?.user.destinationCalendar ? [bookingToDelete?.user.destinationCalendar] : []`. For collective events with multiple hosts, only one destination calendar is present. Calendar services like GoogleCalendarService.deleteEvent use `event.destinationCalendar?.find(...)` fallbacks and BaseCalendarService filters by the first entry — so deletion/update may target the organizer's calendar rather than the calendar where the event actually lives. The evt should aggregate destination calendars from all booking references (each reference has externalCalendarId + credentialId) or the booking should store all destination calendars. As written, cancel/reschedule for collective events can miss the second host's calendar event.

findings.title: Inverted IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED condition drops organization slug when billing is enabled and sets it when disabled
findings.body: The diff changed `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` and `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { requestedSlug: slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { requestedSlug: slug } : {})`. Wait — re-reading: original was `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug }` (slug set when billing DISABLED) and new is `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}` (slug set when billing ENABLED). These are opposite semantics. Combined with the metadata line which kept `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { requestedSlug: slug } : {}`, the new code sets `slug` exactly when `requestedSlug` is set. On self-hosted instances without team billing (IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED=false), organizations would now be created WITHOUT a slug, breaking org subdomain routing (orgDomains relies on team.slug). This looks like an accidental logic inversion unrelated to the destinationCalendar change and will break organization creation on non-billing deployments.

findings.title: buildUIDCalendarEvent throws when users exist instead of when they don't, and then dereferences possibly-undefined mainOrganizer
findings.body: The method `buildUIDCalendarEvent()` starts with `if (this.users && this.users.length > 0) { throw new Error("call buildUsers before calling this function"); }` — the condition is inverted: it throws precisely when users HAVE been built (the correct precondition), and proceeds to `const [mainOrganizer] = this.users;` when users is empty/undefined, making mainOrganizer undefined and causing `mainOrganizer.username` to throw a TypeError. The guard should be `if (!this.users || this.users.length === 0)`. As written, any caller that correctly builds users first will get the error, and any caller that doesn't will crash on the next line.

findings.title: Lark createEvent throws when no destination calendar is set, breaking bookings for users without a destination calendar
findings.body: createEvent does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? []; const calendarId = mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId; if (!calendarId) { throw new Error("no calendar id"); }`. Unlike Google/Office365 services which fall back to the primary calendar, Lark hard-fails when destinationCalendar is empty. Previously the code was `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` which also yielded undefined, but the previous behavior may have been to use a default; regardless, with the new array type, any Lark user without a destination calendar configured (destinationCalendar = []) will now get a thrown error on every booking creation, failing the whole event creation. It should fall back to the primary calendar (e.g. via listCalendars and picking primary) instead of throwing.

findings.title: Calendar interface createEvent signature changed to require credentialId, breaking all other Calendar implementations that don't accept it
findings.body: The `Calendar` interface now declares `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent, credentialId: number): Promise<NewCalendarEventType>`. TypeScript method parameters are bivariant for method declarations, so implementations with fewer parameters (e.g. `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)` in LarkCalendarService, Office365CalendarService, BaseCalendarService in packages/lib/CalendarService.ts) still satisfy the interface — but at runtime, CalendarManager.createEvent (packages/core/CalendarManager.ts line 236) calls `calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)`. For implementations that ignore the second argument, the destination calendar selection inside those services relies on `event.destinationCalendar[0]` (the organizer's), NOT the credential being invoked. This means for collective events, when EventManager iterates destination calendars and calls createEvent with host B's credential, the Lark/Office365/Caldav services will still create the event on the FIRST destination calendar (host A's) rather than the calendar matching the credentialId passed. The interface change is not honored by these implementations, so multi-host support silently degrades to "create N duplicate events on host A's calendar" for non-Google providers. Each implementation must use the credentialId to select the matching destination calendar entry (as GoogleCalendarService now does).

findings.title: createEvent in CalendarManager accepts externalId but passes it into the result instead of using it to select the calendar
findings.body: The new signature is `createEvent(credential, calEvent, externalId?)` and it calls `calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)` — passing credential.id, not externalId. The externalId is only attached to the returned EventResult. For GoogleCalendarService this works because it finds the destination calendar by credentialId. But the externalId parameter (destination.externalId from EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents line 370) is the specific calendar on that credential that should receive the event; by not passing it to the calendar service, services that support multiple calendars per credential (Google, Office365) will always pick the first destinationCalendar entry matching the credentialId, which may not be destination.externalId if a user has multiple destination calendar rows for the same credential. The externalId should be threaded through (e.g. as an additional parameter or by ensuring event.destinationCalendar contains the right entry) so the event lands on the intended calendar.

findings.title: loadUsers rewrite changes behavior for dynamic group bookings and swallows errors into generic 500s
findings.body: The loadUsers function was rewritten with a try/catch that throws `HttpError({ statusCode: 500, message: "Unable to load users" })` for any non-HttpError/non-Prisma error, and it removed the `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the dynamic user query. Downstream code that relied on `user.organization?.slug` for org-aware availability/booking will now see undefined. Also, for the eventTypeId branch, the original code returned `eventType.hosts?.length ? hosts.map(...) : eventType.users || []`; the new code returns `users.length ? users : eventType.users` — when hosts exist but map to an empty array (shouldn't happen, but), behavior differs subtly. More importantly, wrapping everything in a 500 masks real errors (e.g. translation failures) and the removed organization select is a functional regression for organization bookings. These changes are unrelated to the destinationCalendar array migration and should be reverted or justified.

findings.title: isTeamEventType computed with string literals instead of SchedulingType enum
findings.body: `const isTeamEventType = !!eventType.schedulingType && ["COLLECTIVE", "ROUND_ROBIN"].includes(eventType.schedulingType);` uses hardcoded strings instead of the imported SchedulingType enum (SchedulingType.COLLECTIVE / SchedulingType.ROUND_ROBIN). This works only because the enum values are those exact strings, but it's fragile and inconsistent with the rest of the codebase (e.g. confirm.handler.ts uses SchedulingType.COLLECTIVE). If the enum values ever change, this silently breaks. Use the enum.

findings.title: Webhook e2e expectations for destinationCalendar are inconsistent (null vs []) and only one case was updated
findings.body: The BOOKING_REJECTED test was updated to expect `destinationCalendar: []` (line 249), but the BOOKING_CREATED test still expects `destinationCalendar: null` (line 119) and the BOOKING_REQUESTED test still expects `destinationCalendar: null` (line 373). With the new array type, the webhook payload will contain `destinationCalendar: []` (empty array) when no destination calendar is set — `toMatchObject` with `null` will fail because `[]` does not match `null`. These two assertions need to be updated to `[]` as well, otherwise the e2e suite will fail (or the payload actually sends null, which would indicate the evt construction in some paths still produces null and violates the new type). Either way the inconsistency must be resolved.

findings.title: requestReschedule evt.destinationCalendar drops the user's destination calendar fallback
findings.body: The new code is `destinationCalendar: bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar ? [bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar] : []`. The original code was `bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar || bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar` (a no-op fallback to itself, likely a bug, but the booking query at line 60 selects destinationCalendar and the user's destinationCalendar is not selected). Other handlers (handleCancelBooking, confirm.handler) fall back to `user.destinationCalendar` when the booking has none. Here, when the booking has no destinationCalendar, the evt gets an empty array, so downstream calendar deletion (which uses evt.destinationCalendar to locate the calendar) may fail to find the right calendar. The booking query should also select `user: { select: { destinationCalendar: true } }` and the fallback should mirror the other handlers.

findings.title: BrokenIntegrationEmail calendar name derivation can produce "undefined undefined" or crash when integration has no underscore
findings.body: The code does `let calendar = mainHostDestinationCalendar ? mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration.split("_") : "calendar";` then `if (Array.isArray(calendar)) { const calendarCap = calendar.map(...); calendar = calendarCap[0] + " " + calendarCap[1]; }`. If `integration` is a string without an underscore (e.g. "caldav"), split returns a single-element array and `calendarCap[1]` is undefined, producing "Caldav undefined" in the email. If mainHostDestinationCalendar is undefined, calendar stays the string "calendar" and the Array.isArray branch is skipped — OK. But the undefined-second-element case produces broken user-facing text. Should guard `calendarCap[1] ?? ""` or use a proper display name.

findings.title: BaseCalendarService (CalDAV/Apple) createEvent only creates the event on the first destination calendar, ignoring additional hosts' calendars
findings.body: In BaseCalendarService.createEvent, `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? [];` then the calendars filter matches only `c.externalId === mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId` (or all calendars if no externalId). For a collective event with multiple hosts each having their own CalDAV/Apple calendar credential, EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents calls createEvent once per destination entry with a different credential — but each BaseCalendarService instance is constructed with ONE credential (the host's), and `this.listCalendars(event)` returns that host's calendars. The filter then picks only the calendar matching the FIRST destination calendar's externalId, which belongs to a different host/credential. So for host B's credential, the event is either created on no calendar (if externalIds don't match) or on host A's calendar URL using host B's credentials (auth failure). The filter should match by the credential's own calendars (i.e. create on the primary calendar of THIS credential) rather than by the first destination calendar's externalId. This breaks collective events for CalDAV/Apple Calendar users.

findings.title: referencesToCreate externalCalendarId/credentialId now come from result, but for non-calendar results they are undefined, and for calendar results the externalId is the passed-in destination.externalId which may be undefined
findings.body: In create(), referencesToCreate maps `externalCalendarId: isCalendarType ? result.externalId : undefined` and `credentialId: isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`. result.externalId is the `externalId` param of CalendarManager.createEvent, which EventManager passes as `destination.externalId` (line 370) — but only in the `destination.credentialId` branch. In the else branch (line 380) and the no-destinationCalendar fallback (line 391) and the other_calendar branch (line 403), createEvent is called WITHOUT externalId, so result.externalId is undefined. The booking reference then stores externalCalendarId = undefined, meaning on update/delete the calendar service cannot locate the specific calendar and falls back to primary — which may be wrong for users with multiple calendars. Previously the code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId` which had the same issue but at least was consistent. The reference should store the actual external calendar id returned by the calendar service (creationResult) or the destination.externalId in all branches.

findings.title: PayPal webhook evt.destinationCalendar ignores team hosts' calendars, only organizer/booking calendar is used when creating calendar events post-payment
findings.body: In handlePaymentSuccess, the evt is built with `destinationCalendar: booking.destinationCalendar ? [booking.destinationCalendar] : user.destinationCalendar ? [user.destinationCalendar] : []` and then `new EventManager(user)` + `eventManager.create(evt)` is called when the booking was already confirmed. For collective team bookings paid via PayPal, only the organizer's destination calendar is included; other hosts' calendars are not, so calendar events are only created for the organizer. The booking query (lines 57-86) doesn't fetch eventType hosts or their destination calendars. This is the same multi-host gap as handleNewBooking but in the payment-confirmation path — collective paid bookings confirmed via PayPal webhook will miss host calendar events.

findings.title: Stripe webhook evt.destinationCalendar only includes booking/user calendar, missing team hosts for collective paid bookings
findings.body: Both getBooking (line 101-119) and handlePaymentSuccess (line 207-229) build evt.destinationCalendar from only `booking.destinationCalendar || user.destinationCalendar`. For collective team bookings where the organizer is not the only host, the other hosts' destination calendars are not included, so when `eventManager.create(evt)` runs (lines 242, 331), only the organizer's calendar receives the event. The booking query selects `eventType: true` but the hosts' destination calendars are not fetched. Same gap as the PayPal webhook; collective paid bookings confirmed via Stripe will not create calendar events on all hosts' calendars.

findings.title: confirmHandler evt.destinationCalendar only includes booking/user calendar, missing other hosts for collective bookings
findings.body: The evt built in confirmHandler sets `destinationCalendar: booking?.destinationCalendar ? [booking.destinationCalendar] : user.destinationCalendar ? [user.destinationCalendar] : []`. For collective team bookings requiring confirmation, when the organizer confirms, handleConfirmation → EventManager.create runs with only the organizer's destination calendar. Other hosts' calendars are not included, so their calendar events are not created upon confirmation. The booking query (lines 38-91) doesn't fetch eventType hosts or users with their destination calendars. This breaks the multi-host support for collective events that require confirmation.

findings.title: bookingReminder evt.destinationCalendar only includes booking/user calendar, not team hosts
findings.body: The reminder cron builds `selectedDestinationCalendar = booking.destinationCalendar || user.destinationCalendar` and wraps it in an array. For collective team bookings, only one calendar is included. The reminder email itself (sendOrganizerRequestReminderEmail) may not create calendar events, so impact is limited to email content/links, but if any downstream consumer uses evt.destinationCalendar to schedule or display calendar info, hosts are missing. Low impact but inconsistent with the multi-host goal.

findings.title: updateAllCalendarEvents calls updateEvent with possibly-undefined credential when DB lookup fails
findings.body: In the loop over calendarReference (line 504-551), when `reference.credentialId` is set, the code looks up the credential in this.calendarCredentials and falls back to a DB fetch. If both fail (credential deleted, or app slug missing), `credential` stays undefined and line 542 `result.push(updateEvent(credential, event, bookingRefUid, calenderExternalId))` calls updateEvent with undefined. updateEvent (CalendarManager.ts line 272) does `getCalendar(credential)` and `credential.appName` — wait, it accesses `credential.appName` only in the return, but `getCalendar(credential)` with undefined will throw. The throw is caught by the outer try/catch (line 591), which then returns failure results for ALL references, discarding any successful updates from other references in the same batch. A single missing credential should only fail that one reference.

findings.title: Office365 createEvent only targets the first destination calendar; multi-host collective events create duplicate events on the organizer's calendar
findings.body: Office365CalendarService.createEvent uses `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and builds the URL from `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId`. When EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents calls createEvent once per destination calendar entry (each with a different credentialId), the Office365 service ignores the credentialId parameter (the interface now requires it but this implementation's signature is still `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)` — it doesn't even declare the second parameter). So for host B's credential, the service still uses the FIRST destination calendar's externalId (host A's calendar) with host B's access token — either failing auth or creating the event on the wrong calendar. The service must use the credentialId to find the matching destination calendar entry, like GoogleCalendarService does.

findings.title: Office365 updateEvent and deleteEvent ignore externalCalendarId and destinationCalendar entirely, always using /me/calendar/events
findings.body: Office365CalendarService.updateEvent (line 94-109) always uses `/me/calendar/events/${uid}` and deleteEvent (line 111-123) always uses `/me/calendar/events/${uid}`, ignoring both the `externalCalendarId` parameter and `event.destinationCalendar`. For users who have their events on a non-default calendar (which is exactly what destinationCalendar is for), updates and deletes will 404 or hit the wrong calendar. This was pre-existing behavior but becomes more impactful with the multi-destination-calendar change: for collective events, the event may live on a host's non-default Office365 calendar, and update/delete will silently fail to find it. The methods should use externalCalendarId when provided: `/me/calendars/${externalCalendarId}/events/${uid}`.

findings.title: CalendarEventClass.destinationCalendar typed as DestinationCalendar[] but Prisma DestinationCalendar type includes relation fields that may not be present at runtime
findings.body: The class declares `destinationCalendar?: DestinationCalendar[] | null;` using the Prisma model type. However, in many call sites the destination calendar objects come from partial selects (e.g. `user.destinationCalendar` selected without `credential` include, or `booking.destinationCalendar` selected as a scalar relation). The Prisma `DestinationCalendar` type includes all scalar fields, which is fine, but code that does `destination.credentialId` (EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents line 340) relies on credentialId being present — it is a scalar on the model so it's fine. The concern is that `IntegrationCalendar` (used in CalendarManager.getConnectedCalendars) is a different shape, and some code mixes them. The type is technically correct for the Prisma relation but the class is also used with IntegrationCalendar-like objects in places; consider using a narrower type like `Pick<DestinationCalendar, "id" | "externalId" | "integration" | "credentialId">[]` to make the contract explicit. Low severity — more of a type-safety improvement.

findings.title: Only evt.destinationCalendar[0] is connected to the booking; additional hosts' destination calendars are not persisted anywhere on the booking
findings.body: At booking creation, `destinationCalendar: evt.destinationCalendar && evt.destinationCalendar.length > 0 ? { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } } : undefined`. The Booking model has a single `destinationCalendarId` foreign key, so only the first (organizer's) destination calendar is stored. The additional team hosts' destination calendars pushed into evt.destinationCalendar (teamDestinationCalendars) are used during event creation (EventManager.create) but are NOT persisted on the booking. On reschedule or cancel, handlers reconstruct evt.destinationCalendar from `booking.destinationCalendar` (single) — the other hosts' calendars are lost. This means the multi-host calendar support works only for the initial creation; reschedule/cancel will not update/delete events on the other hosts' calendars (unless references are used, but handleCancelBooking's evt construction doesn't aggregate from references). This is a fundamental data-model limitation that the PR does not address — either the Booking model needs a many-to-many relation to DestinationCalendar, or reschedule/cancel must rebuild the destination calendar list from booking references + eventType hosts.
